title: Platinum is a Photocatalyst: Large Visible-Light Quantum Efficiency Revealed
authors: Olivier Henrotte, Yin Chak Wong, Jordan Edwards, Simão Meneses João, Štěpán Kment, Emiliano Cortés, Johannes Lischner, Alberto Naldoni
abstract: Metal-semiconductor junctions in optoelectronic devices are commonly engineered to promote charge separation. In Pt/TiO2 Schottky junctions, Pt is typically regarded as a catalytic electron sink rather than a visible-light-active component. Here, we demonstrate that Pt nanoislands on TiO2 can generate photochemically active carriers under visible light excitation. Using quantitative scanning photoelectrochemical microscopy, we measure the wavelength-resolved external quantum efficiency (EQE) of Au and Pt nanoisland arrays on TiO2, and correlate their reactivity with their morphology and extinction spectra. Discrete 10 nm Pt nanoislands exhibit robust broadband visible light photoactivity - exceeding the photoactivity of similar-sized Au nanoislands under blue-green excitation - whereas Pt's photoactivity is strongly suppressed when the nanoislands are connected. Surprisingly, Pt exhibits an EQE-per-atom approx. 20 times higher than Au at 455 nm and approx. 2 times higher at 595 nm (at Au's optimum). We show an approximately wavelength-independent Pt internal quantum efficiency of approx. 1 percent across the visible spectral region. These findings reposition catalytic metals with strongly damped optical response in the visible as light-responsive components in metal-semiconductor hybrids, challenging the prevailing perception that they function solely as passive co-catalysts in photocatalytic systems.
summary: This research demonstrates that Platinum nanoislands on $	ext{TiO}_2$ are highly efficient photocatalysts under visible light, challenging the view of Pt as merely a passive material. By using advanced photoelectrochemical microscopy and theoretical modeling, the authors show that discrete Pt islands generate photochemically active carriers with efficiencies comparable to or better than Au. The findings reposition noble metals as crucial, light-responsive components in optoelectronic devices.
main_problem: To challenge the view that catalytic metals like Platinum (Pt) are merely passive co-catalysts with poor visible-light quantum efficiency in photocatalysis, especially when compared to Gold (Au).
main_result: Discrete Pt nanoislands exhibit robust broadband visible-light photoactivity, showing an EQE-per-atom significantly higher than Au at specific wavelengths. This reclassifies Pt as a light-responsive component rather than just a passive catalyst.
method: The study combines quantitative scanning photoelectrochemical microscopy (SPECM) measurements with theoretical hot-carrier generation rate calculations.
model_or_system: The system involves metal nanoislands ($	ext{Pt}$ and $	ext{Au}$) deposited on a semiconductor ($	ext{TiO}_2$), forming Schottky junctions. The analysis compares the photoactivity derived from plasmonic excitation in both metals.
key_observables: Wavelength-resolved external quantum efficiency (EQE), EQE per atom, internal quantum efficiency, and local extinction spectra.
important_parameters: Visible light spectral region ($\sim 455 	ext{ nm}$ to $595 	ext{ nm}$); Schottky barrier heights ($\Phi_B$ for $	ext{Au-TiO}_2$ vs. $	ext{Pt-TiO}_2$).
main_assumptions: The hot-carrier model does not explicitly include interfacial electronic states, thermalization losses, or defect-mediated recombination pathways.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SPECM setup, energy band diagrams for both metal/semiconductor junctions, and position-resolved maps comparing Au vs. Pt EQE, correlating activity with morphology and optical properties.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting $	ext{Pt}$'s traditional role with its observed photoactivity. It details the experimental methodology using SPECM to measure wavelength-dependent charge generation ($	ext{EQE}$). Theoretical calculations then link this observation to hot-carrier dynamics, concluding that Pt functions as an active light harvester.
why_interesting: The work bridges concepts from plasmonics and semiconductor physics by quantifying how intrinsic material properties (like the density of states in $	ext{Pt}$) can lead to measurable photoactivity far exceeding simple co-catalyst models. This is relevant for understanding charge separation dynamics at metal/semiconductor interfaces.
